notes.meaning: Jesus crossed over the Sea of Galilee, which was also known as the Sea of Tiberias, to the quieter eastern shore. John records this miracle and journey because it leads directly into Christ's important sermon on the bread of life. Crossing the water also provided a brief rest away from the crowds.

A huge crowd followed Jesus along the shore because they had seen Him heal the sick. Many in the crowd were drawn by curiosity and wonder at His power rather than true faith in their hearts. Still, their eagerness shows how hungry the people were for His help.

Jesus walked up into the hills with His disciples and sat down with them. In those days, a teacher sat down to teach with authority and to receive anyone who wished to come. Sitting on the hillside gave Him a natural place to see and teach the approaching crowds.

The yearly Jewish feast of Passover was drawing near. This festival celebrated how God rescued Israel from Egypt and fed them in the wilderness. Mentioning the feast prepares the reader to see how Jesus provides heavenly bread for His people.

Looking down, Jesus saw the vast multitude streaming toward Him. He turned to Philip and asked where they could buy bread to feed all these people. Because Philip was from a nearby town, he would naturally know the area, but Jesus also wanted to turn the disciples' minds toward God's provision.

Jesus did not ask Philip because He was confused, for He already knew exactly what He would do. He asked the question to test Philip and help him grow in faith. God tests His followers to strengthen their trust in Him, never to lead them into sin.

Philip calculated that two hundred silver coins, equal to more than six months of wages, would not buy even a tiny bite for each person. He looked only at natural limits and the disciples' empty pockets. In his worry, he forgot that the Master of creation was standing right beside him.

Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, spoke to Jesus next. Just as Andrew had previously brought his brother to Christ, he was now ready to bring what little he could find to his Lord. He stepped forward to offer a small piece of information to the group.

Andrew pointed out a young boy who carried five barley loaves and two small fish. Barley was the plain, cheap bread eaten by the poorest people, and the fish were tiny dried or pickled bites. Andrew was willing to mention this small lunch, yet he admitted it was nothing among such a massive crowd.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church father Augustine interpreted the five barley loaves as the five books of Moses (the Old Testament law), the boy as the people of Israel, and the two fish as the priest and the ruler.

notes.meaning: Jesus ordered the disciples to have everyone sit down on the thick spring grass. About five thousand men sat down in organized groups, along with women and children. Like a good shepherd leading his flock to green pastures, Jesus brought calm order to the hungry crowd.

Jesus took the simple food, gave thanks to God, and distributed it through His disciples to the seated crowd. The loaves and fish were miraculously created and multiplied in His hands so that everyone ate as much as they wanted. By giving thanks first, Jesus set an example for us to thank God for every meal.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The multiplication of the loaves directly points ahead to the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper), where Christ feeds His people with an abundance of supernatural, spiritual food.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern writers claim that Jesus did not perform a supernatural miracle of creation, but rather inspired the selfish crowd to pull out and share the lunches they had hidden.

notes.meaning: When everyone was completely satisfied, Jesus commanded the disciples to gather all the leftover pieces so nothing would be wasted. Even though Jesus possessed infinite divine power, He taught that God's bountiful gifts must never be treated carelessly. Plenty of blessings gives no excuse for wastefulness.

The disciples gathered the leftover bread and filled twelve sturdy wicker baskets. This huge amount of surplus food proved that the miracle was genuine, physical, and far greater than their original supply. It also provided each of the twelve disciples with a personal basket of food after their hard work.

After tasting the bread, the people declared that Jesus was truly the Prophet promised to come into the world. They connected this miracle to Moses, who had promised a coming Prophet and fed Israel with manna. However, many in the crowd wanted a political leader rather than a savior from sin.

Jesus realized the crowd planned to seize Him by force and make Him their king, so He retreated alone into the hills. They wanted an earthly monarch who could provide free food and lead a war against the Roman rulers. Jesus refused to let them turn His spiritual mission into a worldly political revolution.

As darkness fell, the disciples headed down from the mountain to the shoreline. Jesus had sent them ahead to get into the boat while He stayed behind to pray. Their journey put them on the path of duty even as the night began.

The disciples boarded the boat and started rowing across the lake toward Capernaum. Complete darkness quickly covered the water, and Jesus had not yet come to them. Being in the dark without their Master made their voyage feel lonely and uncertain.

A fierce wind began to blow, whipping the sea into violent, dangerous waves. The disciples found themselves trapped in a sudden storm in the middle of the lake. Even faithful followers of Christ can face sudden trials while obeying His call.

After struggling at the oars for three or four miles, the disciples saw Jesus walking across the surface of the water toward the boat. Because it was dark and stormy, seeing a figure glide across the waves terrified them, and they feared it was a ghost. Yet Christ came walking on the sea to reveal His power over nature and protect His friends.

Jesus called out through the wind, telling the disciples not to be afraid because it was Him. Hearing the reassuring voice of their Lord turned their sudden terror into deep comfort. Believers find true peace in knowing that Christ is near them in life's darkest storms.

differ.view: Jesus' words ('It is I') are a direct echo of God's holy name ('I AM'), openly displaying His divine power and deity to the disciples.
The phrase was simply a normal self-identification so the frightened disciples would recognize Jesus' voice and stop being afraid.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The words spoken by Jesus on the water connect Him directly with the divine name revealed to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus.

notes.meaning: Once the disciples recognized Jesus, they gladly welcomed Him into their boat. Right away, the boat reached the shore where they were heading. With Christ on board, their frightening struggle ended, and their voyage was brought safely to its end.

The next morning, the crowd that stayed on the eastern shore began looking for Jesus. They remembered that only one small boat had been docked there the night before, and they had seen the disciples row away alone. They knew Jesus had not boarded that vessel.

Other small boats from the city of Tiberias arrived near the spot where the people had eaten the miraculous meal. John reminds his readers that this bread had been eaten after the Lord gave thanks to God. These newly arrived boats gave the crowd a way to travel across the water.

When the crowd realized that neither Jesus nor His disciples were anywhere on that shore, they climbed into the boats and headed to Capernaum to search for Him. Capernaum was the town where Jesus usually stayed during His ministry in Galilee. Although they pursued Him with great effort, their chief desire was to receive more free food and worldly favors.
